So far, we have talked about normal driving, normal conditions. But the road does not always give you normal. Sometimes, the weather turns against you. Sometimes, things go wrong. In this module, we prepare you for those times.

Let us start with adverse weather—the things the sky throws at you.

First, rain. Nigeria knows rain. From April to October, it can pour like the heavens have opened.

The first thirty minutes of rain are the most dangerous. Why? Because the rain mixes with oil and dirt on the road, creating a slippery film. It is like driving on soap.

Action: Reduce your speed by at least one-third. Increase your following distance to four seconds minimum. Turn on your headlights—not just your parking lights, your headlights. Be smooth with everything—steering, braking, accelerating. Jerky movements will lose traction.

In very heavy rain, you may experience hydroplaning. This is when your tyres lose contact with the road and ride on top of the water. You will feel the steering go light—like the car is floating. The engine sound may change.

Action: Do NOT brake. Do NOT turn sharply. Ease off the accelerator gently. Grip the steering wheel firmly. Look where you want to go. Let the car slow down naturally until the tyres grip again.

And please—never drive through flooded roads. You see our brothers driving through water up to their doors? That is not bravery, that is foolishness. Six inches of water can reach your floorboard and stall your engine. One foot of water can float your car. Two feet can carry it away.

If you cannot see the road surface, do not enter.

Next, harmattan fog. December to February, the harmattan wind brings dust and fog. You cannot see far. Distance becomes difficult to judge.

Action: Use your LOW beam headlights. High beams will reflect off the dust and fog and blind you. Reduce your speed so you can stop within the distance you can see. Use the right edge of the road as a guide. If visibility is very bad, pull over completely—off the road—and wait. Do not stop in the travel lane.

Thunderstorms with strong wind. Our rains can bring heavy wind that pushes your vehicle. A sudden gust can move you out of your lane.

Action: Grip the steering wheel firmly. Reduce speed. Be aware of high-sided vehicles—they may sway into your lane. Watch for fallen branches or debris on the road.

Extreme heat. In the dry season, the sun beats down. Your engine works harder. Your tyres build pressure.

Action: Watch your temperature gauge. If it climbs, turn off the air conditioner to reduce engine load. Check your tyre pressures when the tyres are cold—morning is best. Hot tyres will show higher pressure, so do not release air when hot—wait for them to cool.

In all weather conditions, remember to communicate with your passenger. If you are driving slower because of rain, tell them: "The roads are slippery, so I am taking it easy for our safety." A passenger who understands is a passenger who is not worried.

Kunle here. Weather challenges you slowly. But sometimes, the challenge is instant. Next, we talk about emergencies.

MODULE 4, PART 2: Emergency Situations

Welcome back. Kunle again. An emergency on the road gives you no time to think. You must react from training, not from panic. In this section, we will drill the responses until they become automatic.

First, tyre blowout.

Suddenly, BANG! The car pulls hard to one side. Your heart jumps. Your instinct is to slam the brakes and yank the wheel. Do not.

The correct response: Grip, Coast, Steer, Brake.

One, GRIP the steering wheel with both hands—tight, like your life depends on it.

Two, COAST. Take your foot off the accelerator. Do NOT brake yet.

Three, STEER gently. Correct the pull with small movements. Keep the car in your lane.

Four, BRAKE gently. Only when you have control, apply the brakes lightly and guide the car to a safe stop—completely off the road.

Next, brake failure. You push the pedal and it goes to the floor. No resistance. No stopping.

The correct response: Pump, Downshift, Handbrake, Escape.

One, PUMP the brake pedal rapidly. This may build pressure.

Two, DOWNSHIFT. If automatic, shift from D to 3, 2, or L. Let the engine help slow you.

Three, Use the HANDBRAKE gradually. Pull it gently, not suddenly, or the rear wheels may lock.

Four, Look for an ESCAPE ROUTE. A soft shoulder, an uphill slope, a place to roll to a stop.

Stuck accelerator. The engine is screaming. The car will not slow down.

Response: Neutral, Brake, Ignition.

One, Shift to NEUTRAL. The engine will rev wildly, but the car will stop accelerating.

Two, BRAKE firmly and steer to safety.

Three, Turn off the IGNITION once stopped. Do not turn to "lock"—just to "off."

Now, the emergency no one wants: a collision.

If it happens, follow this protocol: Secure, Check, Call, Document, Report.

One, SECURE THE SCENE. If you can move, get out of traffic. Turn on hazards. Put out warning triangles if you have them.

Two, CHECK FOR INJURIES. Yourself, your passengers, others. Do not move injured people unless there is immediate danger like fire.

Three, CALL 911 or the police. Give your location, number of vehicles, any injuries.

Four, DOCUMENT. Take photos—wide shots of the whole scene, close-ups of damage, licence plates, street signs. Get witness contact information. Do not argue about fault. Do not admit blame.

Five, REPORT TO RENTMAIKAR. Call our emergency line immediately. We will guide you through the rest.

Vehicle fire. If you see smoke or flames from the engine:

Pull over immediately. Get everyone out—at least one hundred feet away. Call 911. Do NOT open the bonnet—it feeds oxygen to the fire. Only use a fire extinguisher if the fire is very small and you are trained.

Medical emergency. If a passenger becomes ill:

Pull over safely. Ask if they need medical help. Call 911 if needed. Use your first aid kit only if you are trained. Follow the dispatcher's instructions.

Unsafe passenger. If a passenger is aggressive, threatening, or intoxicated to the point of being a risk:

Stop in a safe, public place. Politely ask them to exit. If they refuse, call 911. Your safety comes first. Always.

Kunle here. Emergencies test your skills. But your daily work tests your character. In our final section, we talk about the human side of driving—customer service and professionalism.

MODULE 4, PART 3: Customer Service & Professionalism

Welcome back. Kunle again. You have reached the final section of this training.

You have learned about defensive driving. You have learned about vehicle safety and maintenance. You have learned about emergencies. But there is one more thing that makes a great Rentmaikar driver: how you treat people.

For every passenger, you ARE Rentmaikar. They do not see the company office. They do not see the managers. They see YOU. Your smile, your professionalism, your care—that is the Rentmaikar experience.

Let us start with safety-first service.

Before you even say hello, do a quick check. Is this the right passenger? "Good afternoon, sir/madam. Rentmaikar for destination?"

Then, before you move, check seatbelts. "Please, for your safety, make sure your seatbelt is fastened." For the back seat too. For everyone. If someone refuses? You can refuse the trip. Safety is not optional.

Professional conduct.

Your appearance matters. Clean Rentmaikar attire. A neat appearance says, "I take my job seriously."

Your vehicle matters. Clean inside and out. No rubbish on the floor. No strange smells. A clean car is a professional car.

Your communication matters. Be polite. "Please," "thank you," "sir," "ma." These small words cost nothing but mean everything.

Special situations.

Intoxicated passenger. If someone has had too much to drink, you may refuse service. If they are already in the car and become a problem, stop in a safe, public place. Politely end the trip. Document in the app.

Lost items. If you find something left behind, stop accepting trips. Report it through the app immediately with a description and photo. Secure it in your trunk. Follow the return procedure exactly.

Complaints. If a passenger is unhappy, listen first. Do not interrupt. Say, "I understand why you feel that way." Apologise for the situation: "I am sorry this has happened." Then report it properly. Do not argue. Do not get defensive.

Now, let us talk about YOU. Your health and well-being matter.

Fatigue management. If you are tired, you are dangerous. Know the signs: heavy eyelids, yawning, missing your turn, drifting in your lane. When you feel tired, take a break. Stop at a safe place. Walk around. Get fresh air. Do not push through.

Stress. This job can be stressful—traffic, passengers, deadlines. Breathe deeply. Listen to calm music. Remember that you control your driving. A calm driver is a safe driver.

Posture. Adjust your seat so you can reach everything comfortably. Your back should be supported. Take care of your body—it is the only one you have.

My brother, my sister. You have completed this training.

You are not just a driver. You are a safety professional. You are a vehicle caretaker. You are a calm presence in emergencies. You are the face of Rentmaikar.

Every time you get behind the wheel, remember:

Aim high in steering. Get the big picture. Keep your eyes moving. Leave an out. Make sure they see you.

Check your vehicle. Listen to its messages. Respect the weather. Handle emergencies with calm. And treat every passenger like a guest in your own home.

You are Rentmaikar. Drive with pride. Drive with care. Drive safely.

This is Kunle. God bless you. God bless your journeys. And we will see you on the road.
